In this notebook you will explore individual workplace injuries and illnesses that
employers reported to OSHA through the Injury Tracking Application (ITA).
Read the module [README](../README.md) and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

By default this notebook uses the **sample** (5,000 random cases from each year, 2023 to 2025),
which is committed to the repository. To use the **full** data, run
`scripts/fetch_data.R` first and set `use_full_data <- TRUE`.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

use_full_data <- FALSE

raw_dir <- "../data/raw"
sample_path <- "../data/sample/ita_case_detail_sample.csv"
sample_url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/",
                     "main/modules/us-osha-ita-case-detail/data/sample/ita_case_detail_sample.csv")

read_ita <- function(path) {
  df <- read_csv(path, col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), progress = FALSE)
  names(df) <- tolower(trimws(names(df)))
  # The 2023 file calls this column year_filing_for; later years use year_of_filing
  names(df)[names(df) == "year_filing_for"] <- "year_of_filing"
  df
}

if (use_full_data) {
  files <- list.files(raw_dir, pattern = "\\.(csv|zip)$", ignore.case = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)
  if (length(files) == 0) stop("No files in ", raw_dir, ". Run scripts/fetch_data.R first.")
  ita <- bind_rows(lapply(files, function(f) mutate(read_ita(f), source_file = basename(f))))
} else {
  # Falls back to the copy on GitHub if the sample is not on your computer
  ita <- read_ita(if (file.exists(sample_path)) sample_path else sample_url)
}

cat(format(nrow(ita), big.mark = ","), "cases,", ncol(ita), "columns\n")
```

Column names differ slightly between years (for example, the 2025 file does not have the
OIICS codes yet). `pick()` finds the first name that exists.

```{r columns}
pick <- function(...) {
  candidates <- c(...)
  found <- intersect(candidates, names(ita))
  if (length(found) == 0) {
    message("None of ", paste(candidates, collapse = ", "),
            " found. Check names(ita) against the data dictionary.")
    return(NA_character_)
  }
  found[1]
}

outcome_col   <- pick("incident_outcome")
days_away_col <- pick("dafw_num_away")
type_col      <- pick("type_of_incident")
naics_col     <- pick("naics_code")
state_col     <- pick("state")
soc_col       <- pick("soc_description", "soc_code")
year_col      <- pick("year_of_filing", "source_file")

outcome_labels <- c("1" = "Death", "2" = "Days away from work",
                    "3" = "Job transfer or restriction", "4" = "Other recordable case")
type_labels <- c("1" = "Injury", "2" = "Skin disorder", "3" = "Respiratory condition",
                 "4" = "Poisoning", "5" = "Hearing loss", "6" = "All other illnesses")
```

# Part 2. How serious are these cases?

```{r outcomes}
ita <- ita |>
  mutate(outcome = coalesce(unname(outcome_labels[.data[[outcome_col]]]), "Unknown/missing"),
         case_type = coalesce(unname(type_labels[.data[[type_col]]]), "Unknown/missing"))

ita |>
  count(outcome, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))

ggplot(ita, aes(y = fct_rev(fct_infreq(outcome)))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Cases by most serious outcome", x = "Number of cases", y = NULL)

count(ita, case_type, sort = TRUE)
```

**Questions**

1. What share of cases involved days away from work? Job transfer or restriction?
2. Illnesses make up a small share of cases. Give two reasons why work-related
   illnesses are probably under-recorded on OSHA logs.

**Your answer:**



# Part 3. Days away from work

```{r days-away}
days <- ita |>
  mutate(days_away = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.data[[days_away_col]]))) |>
  filter(days_away > 0)

summary(days$days_away)
sum(days$days_away > 180)

ggplot(days, aes(x = pmin(days_away, 180))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  labs(title = "Days away from work (capped at 180)", x = "Days", y = "Cases")
```

**Questions**

1. Compare the mean and median. What does the difference tell you about the shape of the distribution?
2. OSHA recordkeeping rules say employers may stop counting days away at 180 for a single case.
   How many cases in the data are above 180? What does that suggest about data quality, and
   how would you handle these values?

**Your answer:**



# Part 4. Who and where?

NAICS codes are hierarchical. The first two digits give the industry sector
(for example 23 = construction, 31 to 33 = manufacturing, 48 to 49 = transportation and
warehousing, 62 = health care and social assistance).

```{r who-where}
ita <- mutate(ita, naics_2 = str_sub(.data[[naics_col]], 1, 2))

count(ita, naics_2, sort = TRUE) |> head(10)
count(ita, .data[[soc_col]], sort = TRUE) |> head(15)
if (!is.na(state_col)) count(ita, .data[[state_col]], sort = TRUE) |> head(10)
```

**Questions**

1. Which sectors and occupations account for the most cases?
2. Many cases have an occupation of "Uncoded" or "Insufficient Information - NIOSH". Look at
   some `job_description` values for those cases. Why might the autocoder fail, and how could
   that bias a comparison between occupations?
3. Does having the most cases mean an industry is the *most dangerous*? What would you need
   to know to compare risk between industries? (Hint: see "incidence rate" in the data dictionary.)

**Your answer:**



# Part 5. What happened? (OIICS codes)

BLS used an autocoder to assign **Occupational Injury and Illness Classification System
(OIICS)** codes to each case from the narratives: the *event* (how the injury happened), the
*nature* (what the injury was), the *part of body*, and the *source* (what caused it).
Only 2-digit codes were assigned. The 2025 file does not have OIICS codes yet; OSHA adds them
after the year is complete.

```{r oiics}
ita |>
  filter(!is.na(event_title_pred)) |>
  count(.data[[year_col]], event_title_pred, sort = TRUE) |>
  group_by(.data[[year_col]]) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)
```

**Questions**

1. What are the three most common events? Are they what you expected?
2. Compare the event labels for 2023 and 2024. Do they use the same wording? What would you
   need to check before comparing OIICS categories across years?

**Your answer:**



# Part 6. Reading the narratives

Form 301 asks the employer to describe what happened in their own words. Find the
narrative columns and search them for a hazard of your choice.

```{r narratives}
narrative_cols <- str_subset(names(ita), "^new_")  # "new_" marks fields OSHA redacted for privacy
narrative_cols

keyword <- "heat"   # try: ladder, forklift, lifting, needle, slip, chemical, violence

narrative_text <- ita |>
  select(all_of(narrative_cols)) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) coalesce(x, ""))) |>
  apply(1, paste, collapse = " ") |>
  str_to_lower()

hits <- ita[str_detect(narrative_text, fixed(keyword)), ]
cat(nrow(hits), "cases mention", keyword,
    sprintf("(%.1f%% of cases)\n", 100 * nrow(hits) / nrow(ita)))
head(select(hits, all_of(narrative_cols)), 10)
```

**Questions**

1. Read 10 matching narratives. How many actually describe the hazard you searched for?
   What does that tell you about keyword searches as a surveillance method?
2. Pick one hazard. Using the hierarchy of controls, propose one control that would have
   prevented two of the cases you read.

**Your answer:**



# Part 7. From counts to rates

Counts tell you where cases are, not where risk is highest. A rate needs a denominator.
Each case row repeats its establishment's `total_hours_worked` from the 300A summary, so
**do not sum hours across cases**. Take one row per establishment instead.

$$\text{DART rate} = \frac{\text{cases with days away, restriction, or transfer} \times 200{,}000}{\text{total hours worked}}$$

```{r rates}
rate_year <- "2024"   # hours worked are reported per year, so compute one year at a time

estab <- ita |>
  filter(.data[[year_col]] == rate_year) |>
  group_by(establishment_id, naics_2) |>
  summarise(
    dart_cases = sum(.data[[outcome_col]] %in% c("2", "3")),
    hours = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(first(total_hours_worked))),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

estab |>
  filter(hours > 0) |>
  group_by(naics_2) |>
  summarise(establishments = n(), dart_cases = sum(dart_cases), hours = sum(hours)) |>
  mutate(dart_rate = round(dart_cases * 200000 / hours, 2)) |>
  filter(establishments >= 20) |>
  arrange(desc(dart_rate))
```

**Questions**

1. If you run this on the **sample**, the rates are far too low. Why? (Hint: what fraction of
   each establishment's cases is in the sample?) Rerun it with the full data.
2. Even with the full data, establishments that had **zero** cases are missing from this file.
   Which direction does that bias the rates? How would the ITA **300A summary** file, linked by
   `establishment_id`, fix it?
3. This dataset only includes establishments with 100+ employees in designated industries.
   How might that selection affect rates compared with BLS's national SOII estimates?
4. Propose a research question that this dataset could answer and that aggregated BLS
   tables could not.

**Your answer:**
